That boy, the reigning breath-holding champion, Kenji Takezo, surrendered his title this year to Mack Stanton, a retired truck driver newly arrived in town. The contest, held at the municipal swimming pool, drew thirty-five participants, who inhaled deeply in unison and submerged to the depths.

The competition stretched into twilight. One by one, each contestant surfaced, gasping for air. Kenji was the town's favorite—we all longed for his victory. He had trained relentlessly; breath-holding was his one true gift, aside from surfing and stirring up mischief.

When he finally emerged, second to last, gulping at the night air before retching up water, our disappointment was palpable. He had been faring so well. His lucky twenty-pound brick rested in his lap throughout, anchoring him to the depths.

But the trucker, Mack, proved unbeatable. Underwater, he had been reading comic books aloud, his laughter rippling to the surface as we watched from the bleachers, captivated.

Kenji noticed this too. No one had ever read to him—not even his mother—and suddenly he yearned to know what words could summon such laughter, what his rival had found so irresistibly funny.

# The Breath-Holding Contest

Kenji Takezo, our reigning breath-holding champion, surrendered his crown this season to Mack Stanton, a newcomer to town who'd recently retired from truck driving. The competition took place at the municipal pool, where thirty-five contenders filled their lungs simultaneously and sank beneath the surface together.

As dusk settled in, the match stretched on. Contestants emerged one at a time, breaking the surface and gasping for air. Everyone in town had been rooting for Kenji—he was our hometown hero. His rigorous training represented the one genuine skill he possessed, aside from his surfing abilities and his knack for causing trouble.

When he finally broke through the water, second-to-last, choking on the evening air before throwing up pool water, we felt let down. He'd seemed unstoppable. Resting on his lap was his fortunate twenty-pound brick, the weight that anchored him beneath the surface. Yet Mack Stanton proved unbeatable.

The truck driver's secret? He recited comic books out loud while submerged. Watching from the stands, we could see bubbles of his laughter rising to the surface. Kenji noticed this too. Nobody had ever read aloud to him before—not even his own mother—and suddenly he found himself desperate to know what story was being told, what joke had his rival laughing underwater.

# The Day the Town Lost Its Breath

For as long as anyone could remember, Kenji Takezo had been the undisputed king of holding his breath. It wasn't much of a talent, some might say, but in this town, it was practically a birthright—passed down through generations of local legend, whispered about at the diner, and celebrated every summer at the annual contest. This year, however, everything changed. Kenji Takezo, the town's beloved breath-holding champion, was dethroned by a most unlikely challenger: Mack Stanton, a retired truck driver who had only recently rolled into town with more stories than possessions.

The contest, as always, took place at the town swimming pool, where thirty-five hopeful participants gathered at the water's edge. Each competitor clutched a twenty-pound brick—the great equalizer that kept even the most buoyant hopefuls anchored to the pool floor. As the sun began its slow descent, the group submerged together in a wave of splashes and held breaths, sinking into a silence that stretched longer than anyone expected. The competition dragged on into twilight, the sky bruising into purples and oranges as, one by one, exhausted faces broke the surface, gasping for air.

Kenji had trained hard for this moment, running through his usual regimen of lung exercises and meditation techniques he'd read about online. But when he finally broke the surface, it was second to last—not the triumphant return he'd envisioned. He gulped desperately at the air, his body betraying him as he doubled over and vomited pool water onto the concrete. The crowd's collective sigh of disappointment was palpable. Breath-holding was Kenji's one true talent, the thing that set him apart from the ordinary the way surfing and causing minor trouble around town could never quite manage. Without it, who was he, really?

But it was what happened next that truly stole the show. Mack Stanton, still submerged, was doing something no one had ever attempted in the contest's long history: he was reading comic books underwater, his voice a muffled rumble beneath the surface. And then, impossibly, laughter—rich, genuine laughter—bubbled up through the water, rising in silvery streams that had the crowd leaning forward from their seats on the bleachers, transfixed. He surfaced last, still chuckling, comic book pages dripping in his weathered hands, utterly unbothered by his victory.

It was in that moment, watching Mack's easy joy ripple across the pool's surface, that something shifted in Kenji. A strange, unexpected ache settled in his chest—not from his oxygen-starved lungs, but from someplace deeper. He realized, with startling clarity, that no one had ever read to him. Not his mother, not his father, not anyone. There had been no bedtime stories, no shared laughter over silly words or absurd plots. And now, staring at this stranger who had bested him not through discipline or lung capacity, but through sheer, uncomplicated delight, Kenji felt an inexplicable longing rise within him.

He wanted to know what had been so funny. He wanted, more than anything, to hear it too.
outputs.L4:
# The Last Bubble

The Willowbrook Municipal Pool smelled like chlorine and ambition every August, when the town held its annual breath-holding contest. For three years running, that ambition had a name: Kenji Takezo, sixteen years old, perpetually in trouble, and possessed of exactly one talent that anyone could point to with pride.

"He can't read good, he can't play ball, but that boy can hold his breath like nobody's business," old Pete Hollins liked to say down at the hardware store, and nobody argued. Kenji's mother had stopped attending parent-teacher conferences years ago, tired of hearing about detentions and missed homework, but she never missed the contest. It was the one day a year when people looked at her son and saw a champion instead of a problem.

This year, though, there was competition. Mack Stanton had rolled into Willowbrook in June, retired from thirty years of long-haul trucking, with a trailer home parked at the edge of town and a peculiar habit that had the whole community talking. He read comic books. Underwater.

Nobody quite understood how he did it—something about controlled exhales, air pockets in his cheeks, decades of practice holding his breath through mountain passes when the cab filled with diesel fumes. But there he was, every Tuesday and Thursday evening, sinking to the bottom of the deep end with a waterproof comic book, his lips moving, sometimes his shoulders shaking with silent laughter, bubbles rising in strange, joyful patterns.

"He's reading to the fish," kids would whisper, pressing their faces against the pool's underwater viewing window that Mr. Hollins had installed years ago for swim lessons. And they weren't entirely wrong—Mack seemed to be reading to someone, some invisible audience, delighting in whatever adventures Archie or Superman or the Fantastic Four were having, forty years of retirement giving him all the time in the world for the stories he'd never had time to read on the road.

The contest was scheduled for the last Saturday before school started. Kenji arrived with his lucky brick—a twenty-pound chunk of concrete he'd found at a construction site three summers ago, the one he always held to keep himself submerged, to keep himself steady, to keep himself from floating up too soon.

"You'll take him easy," said Danny Ochoa, clapping Kenji on the shoulder. "Old man's probably got weak lungs from all that trucking."

Kenji nodded, but he'd seen Mack in the water. He'd seen how still the man could be, how his laughter turned into something like meditation, how he seemed to disappear into whatever world was printed on those colorful pages.

The whistle blew. Both contestants went under. The crowd gathered around the pool's edge, some kids pressing against the underwater window, watching Kenji settle to the bottom with his brick, watching Mack sink down with his comic book, already smiling before he'd even opened it.

Thirty seconds. A minute. Two minutes. The usual challengers surfaced one by one, gasping, disqualified, until only the two remained: the champion with his brick, the newcomer with his story.

Three minutes. Kenji's chest began to ache in that familiar way, the way he knew how to sit with, how to breathe around internally even when he wasn't breathing at all. He'd trained his body to want air less than his mind wanted to win. But something else was happening today, something he hadn't accounted for.

He could see Mack's face in profile, lit by the wavering sunlight through the water. The man's eyes were moving across the page. His mouth was shaping words Kenji couldn't hear. And then—Mack laughed. A real laugh, silent in the water but visible in every line of his body, his shoulders shaking, bubbles bursting from his nose in a happy cascade.

Kenji had never heard someone laugh like that at something read aloud. Not once. Not his mother, not his teachers, not the aides at school who handed him worksheets and sighed. Nobody had ever read to him like there was something worth laughing about, worth sharing, worth surfacing for except to breathe.

Four minutes. His lungs burned. His lucky brick sat heavy in his hands, exactly as it always did, exactly as it should. He was going to win. He knew he was going to win.

But he wanted to know what was so funny.

The thought arrived without permission, curling up from somewhere beneath his competitive drive, beneath three years of being the champion, beneath the only thing he was good at. He wanted to hear the joke. He wanted someone to read to him the way Mack was reading to himself, with that kind of joy, that kind of patience, that kind of love for a story that it spilled out even underwater, even alone, even for an audience of nobody.

Kenji's grip loosened on the brick.

He surfaced second-to-last, gasping, the crowd's collective breath catching as they realized what was happening. Mack came up moments later, comic book still miraculously dry in its plastic sleeve, laughing for real now, in the air, at whatever had struck him as so hilarious three feet underwater.

"Sorry, sorry," Mack said, wiping his eyes, not realizing yet that he'd won. "You ever read this issue? Old Reed Richards gets himself into the darndest—"

He stopped. Looked at Kenji's face. Looked at the crowd's stunned silence, the way they were staring at the two of them, doing math, understanding that the streak was over.

"Oh," Mack said quietly. "I won, didn't I."

Kenji nodded, treading water, unable to explain even to himself why he'd let go, why curiosity had outweighed victory, why some hunger he hadn't known he carried had surfaced faster than his lungs demanded.

That evening, as the pool emptied and the sun began to set, Mack found Kenji sitting on the edge of the shallow end, feet in the water, brick nowhere in sight.

"You want to know what was so funny?" Mack asked, settling down beside him with the careful movements of a man whose knees remembered thirty years of truck cabs.

Kenji shrugged, which meant yes.

Mack opened the comic book, still slightly damp at the edges, and began to read aloud—not underwater this time, but in the ordinary air, in an ordinary voice that nonetheless carried something extraordinary in it: the simple willingness to share a story with someone who wanted to hear it.

Kenji listened. He didn't understand every word, didn't follow every plot point, but he understood the laughter when it came, understood the pause Mack left for him to laugh too, understood that this—this reading aloud, this attention, this small ordinary gift—was something he'd been thirsty for far longer than four minutes underwater could account for.

He'd lost his title. He found he didn't mind nearly as much as he'd expected to.
outputs.L5:
# The Meeting at Dawn

That morning, mist clung to the mountain paths like memories refusing to fade. Kenji walked slowly, his wooden staff tapping against the stone steps of the old shrine. He had traveled three days to reach this place, carrying with him a promise made long ago.

Takezo was already waiting beneath the ancient cedar tree, exactly as the letter had said he would be. His posture was still, disciplined—the mark of years spent training in solitude. When Kenji approached, neither spoke at first. That silence between them held more weight than any words could carry.

"You came," Takezo finally said, not turning around.

"I said I would," Kenji replied.

That single exchange seemed to dissolve years of distance between them. They had once been students together, sharing the same teacher, the same dreams of mastering the way of the sword. But paths diverge, and circumstances change people in ways neither had expected.

Takezo turned to face his old friend. The years had carved lines into his face, but his eyes remained sharp, watchful. "Do you still practice?"

"Every day," Kenji answered. "That discipline never left me, even when everything else did."

They stood together as the sun broke through the mist, illuminating the shrine grounds in gold. Whatever had brought them to this reunion—whatever debts of honor or unfinished business remained between Kenji and Takezo—could wait a little longer. For now, it was enough to simply stand together again, two old friends reunited by fate and time.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal short poem about a small-town breath-holding contest and the underdog who loses his title.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Breath-Holding Contest

Every August, the town gathers
at the lake gone flat as a held tongue,
where Municipal Referee Vance
counts seconds with his one good arm,
and the water refuses to ripple, out of respect.

Duncan Pryor held the record eleven years—
four minutes, sixteen seconds,
his lungs like church bells that never rang,
his face beneath the surface serene
as a man reading mail that isn't his.

But this year the new boy came,
skin pale as unlit birthday candles,
and sank without a bubble,
sank like he'd been practicing
in his mother's amniotic fluid,
sank until the crowd forgot
what breathing was invented for.

Five minutes. The dragonflies stopped their engines.
Six minutes. Someone's casserole went cold
three streets over, in sympathy.

Duncan surfaced first,
gasping like a screen door,
and watched the boy rise slow,
not desperate—*disappointed*,
as if the air itself
had let him down
by insisting he return.

They pinned the ribbon on the boy's wet shirt.
It bled blue down his collarbone
like a vein finally giving up its secret.

Duncan walked home past the Baptist church,
past his own reflection in shop windows
gasping soundlessly beside him,
and thought: *eleven years*
*I was the town's cathedral of lungs*,
*now I'm just a man who breathes*
*like everybody else*,

ordinary as a mailbox,
ordinary as the tide
that doesn't care
who almost became the sea.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a free-verse narrative poem featuring quirky characters like a champion breath holder and a retired truck driver who beats him.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Beaumont County Fair Breath-Holding Championship**

Dewey Calloway could hold his breath for four minutes and eleven seconds,
a fact he wore like a medal made of lung tissue,
telling anyone who'd listen about the time in Tulsa
when the judges had to check his pulse with a stethoscope
because they thought he'd gone and died correctly.

He trained for this. Had a regimen.
Meditation tapes. A diet free of carbonation.
He'd float face-down in his above-ground pool
like a man rehearsing his own drowning,
counting Mississippis with the patience of a monk.

Nobody expected Earl Prewitt to enter.
Earl, who'd driven eighteen-wheelers for thirty-one years
hauling frozen chickens from Arkansas to Reno,
who showed up in the same flannel shirt he wore to church,
who signed the entry sheet with the stub of pencil
they use for scoring miniature golf.

The crowd laughed, not unkindly.
Earl was sixty-eight and built like a mailbox,
the kind of man who apologizes to furniture
when he bumps into it.

"You ever done this before?" the judge asked.

"Nope," Earl said. "But I've waited on loading docks
in Beaumont, Texas, in August,
for six hours once, engine off, no radio,
watching a forklift break down four separate times.
I figure I know something about
holding still inside myself."

Dewey went first, of course. Champions go first.
He dropped into the dunk tank like a man
returning to the womb, cheeks puffed like a trumpeter,
and the crowd started counting.

*One-Mississippi. Two-Mississippi.*

At two minutes his fingers started drumming on his thighs,
a nervous tell nobody caught but his ex-wife,
who'd come to watch, unable to help herself,
the way you can't look away from your old life
even after you've moved out of it completely.

At three-fifty he surfaced, gasping,
setting what would still be, technically, a record—
if records mattered more than what came next.

Earl climbed in without ceremony.
No stretching. No prayer to any water god.
He just sat down like a man settling into a recliner
after a long shift, closed his eyes,
and went somewhere.

The crowd counted past Dewey's time
and something shifted in the air—
not excitement exactly, but a kind of reverence,
the sound a room makes when it realizes
it's watching something it doesn't understand.

Four minutes. Four-thirty. Five.

Dewey stood at the edge of the tank,
his four minutes and eleven seconds
evaporating behind him like a rumor,
watching this soft, unremarkable man
prove that discipline isn't always loud,
that some people learn patience
not from monks or manuals
but from waiting rooms, and rest stops,
and marriages that taught them
how to be alone inside a crowd,
how to survive long stretches
where nothing happens
and nothing is supposed to.

At five minutes forty seconds
Earl came up slow, like a man
surfacing from a nap he'd earned,
and asked what time it was—
not out of showmanship,
but because he genuinely
hadn't been counting.

"I wasn't holding my breath," he explained later,
toweling off, embarrassed by the applause.
"I was just waiting for something to be over.
Forgot to breathe in the meantime.
Forty years of hauling freight'll do that to a man—
teach him the difference
between running out of air
and simply not needing it yet."

Dewey shook his hand, gracious in defeat,
already composing the story he'd tell in Tulsa
about the trucker who out-stilled a champion,
who turned decades of loading-dock boredom
into something like transcendence,
who proved, without meaning to,
that the deepest breath you'll ever hold
might be the one you didn't know
you were taking—

just a man, sitting quiet in the dark water,
waiting, the way he'd always waited,
for the world to tell him
it was time to come back up.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a whimsical, slightly absurdist poem about a local competition where someone reads comic books underwater.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Bubbling Book Club Championship

Down at the municipal pool on Third,
where chlorine fumes make eyes go blurred,
they hold each June the strangest sport:
the Underwater Comics Court.

Contestants wear their swimming trunks,
their goggles fogged, their courage chunks,
and clutch a waxed and laminated
*Spider-Man* (slightly outdated).

The rules are simple, if bizarre:
you dive down deep, you don't go far,
you read three panels, mind the pressure,
and surface with your reading treasure.

Old Gerald Pumpkinwhistle Snoot
has held the title, absolute,
for seven years of soggy glory,
speed-reading tales of derring story.

Judges perch on floating chairs
(inflatable flamingos, pairs)
and squint through masks to verify
the pages turned, the reader's eye

did truly scan each inked-out word
(this claim is often quite absurd,
since no one's sure how eyes can read
when chlorinated bubbles bleed

across the page in blurry storms—
but tradition has its arcane norms).

The prize: a trophy, gold and cheap,
shaped like a fish that's fast asleep,
and bragging rights at the Frost Freeze Diner
where Gerald orders something finer

than the usual grilled cheese—
a sundae, please, with jimmies, please—
while dripping still, in victory's glow,
the *Underwater Comics Pro*.

So if you find this passion odd,
some superhero-loving squad
who reads their Marvel wet and blue—
well, friend, that's just what small towns do.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a poem with vivid, odd details—like a lucky twenty-pound brick—about a town's beloved contestant losing to a newcomer.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Runner-Up

Old Meridian Falls had never seen
a streak like Duffy Trent's—eleven years
of blue rosettes, the county fair's own king
of pickled beets and prize-winning steers.

He kept a twenty-pound brick for luck,
worn smooth as soap from thirty years of rubbing,
inherited from a great-aunt who swore
it once stopped a runaway wagon by simply being there, stubborn.

The newcomer arrived in a Buick the color of a healing bruise,
introduced herself as Vesper Coyne,
and entered nothing but a jar of jam
made from fruit nobody could name—

not quite plum, not quite something
that grows in the dark. The judges wept.
One claimed to taste his childhood dog.
Another swore the jam had somehow slept

inside a cello for a hundred years.
Duffy's beets, that year, tasted only of dirt
and honest labor, which is to say:
they tasted like defeat, like being hurt

in a way too small to name in public.
The brick sat heavy in his coat.
He'd rubbed it raw that morning, prayed
to whatever gods preside over goats

and gourds and the small mercies of blue ribbon,
but Vesper's jam had already won
before the judging—won the way a comet
wins against the sun: by simply outshining, by being done

with waiting in the wings. The town, ever fickle,
already loved her strange, unnameable fruit.
They named a street for her by Tuesday.
Duffy went home, brick in hand, listened to it,

as if it might apologize, or explain
why luck sometimes leaves without a word,
packs its things into a purple Buick,
and drives off chasing something stranger, something blurred

at the edges—the way all good luck eventually is:
a story told so often it becomes a kind of myth,
a brick that maybe never worked at all,
just something heavy to hold onto, something to be with.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a narrative poem in a plainspoken, wry tone about community pride, competition, and unexpected emotional vulnerability.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Founders Day Bake-Off**

Every October the folding tables come out
behind the Grange hall, and Carol Vance
sets up her name placard like she's running
for something, because in a way she is.

Twelve years running, Carol's won Best Pie,
and twelve years running, Marlene Ford
has come in second, which everyone agrees
is its own kind of achievement, if you squint.

This is a town where we take our competitions
seriously precisely because nothing
is actually at stake. The prize is a ribbon
and the right to feel superior at church
for exactly one Sunday before people forget.

I've judged this thing for six years now,
mostly because nobody else wants the job,
and it's taught me that peach cobbler
is a battlefield, that lattice crust
is a philosophy, that a soggy bottom
can end a friendship that started in kindergarten.

This year Marlene's pie was different.
Not better, necessarily—the crumb topping
was a little heavy-handed, the apples
cut too thick in places—but there was something
in it I couldn't score on the sheet.

I found out after, from her daughter,
that Marlene's husband Del had died in March,
that this was the pie he used to request
every year for his birthday, that she'd made it
alone in that kitchen for the first time
without him stealing tastes from the bowl.

She didn't say any of this at the table.
She just set the pie down like it weighed
more than pie should weigh, and went to stand
by the coffee urn, not really looking
at anyone.

Carol won again. Of course she did.
Her crust was, technically, flawless.
But when they called the second place,
and Marlene walked up smiling that smile
you learn to make for occasions,
something shifted in the room—

a quiet you could feel, the way you feel
weather changing before it changes,
and Carol, ribbon in hand, did something
I'd never seen her do in twelve years
of pageantry and pie:

she walked over, hugged Marlene
right there by the coffee urn,
didn't say anything either,
and for a second the whole gymnasium—
folding chairs, bad fluorescent light,
the smell of a hundred kinds of sugar—

held still like it was listening
to something none of us
could quite say out loud,

which was only this:
that we come here every year
pretending it's about the pie,
when it was always about
proving we're still here,
still baking, still showing up
for each other in the ways
we know how, which is to say—

badly, competitively, with too much cinnamon,
but showing up all the same.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
